examples.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Whose Denominator Contains a Leading Coefficient
examples.worked_solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $2$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{2x-1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{x-1}{2(x-\frac{1}{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{x-1}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

|  | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{red}\dfrac12$ | $1$ | $-1$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $\dfrac12$ |
|  | $1$ | $-\dfrac12$ |

So, from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-1}{(x-\frac{1}{2})} & =1-\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(x-\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{2(x-\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{2x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{2x-1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int (1-\frac{1}{2x-1})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[x-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|]+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
We first need to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder parts, which we can do using synthetic division.

We draw up a synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -2 & 1 & -3 & -1 & 2 \\  & ↓ & -2 & 10 & -18 \\  & 1 & -5 & 9 & -16\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-x+2}{x+2}={x}^{2}-5x+9-\frac{16}{x+2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-x+2}{x+2}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}-5x+9-\frac{16}{x+2})\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-5\int x\,\text{d}x+9\int \text{d}x-16\int \frac{1}{x+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{5}{2}{x}^{2}+9x-16\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+C.\end{aligned}
$$
